title: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving
hook: the Forgiving, again and again, however often you return

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Musawwir: the Fashioner who shaped every face, and who looks at hearts, not forms. Your line was every face shaped.

The same old thing. A temper that flares at the same person. A habit quit eleven times. A promise to oneself broken every Tuesday. The first time, asking forgiveness comes easily. By the fifth, it can feel embarrassing. By the twentieth, a person might stop asking at all, sure there's a limit and sure they've hit it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about exactly this person: a servant who does the same wrong again and again, and keeps coming back. Bukhari and Muslim both record it, and the answer is a name built for repetition. Today: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving.
screen: `THE SAME OLD THING.` → `THE TWENTIETH TIME.` → `SURELY THERE'S A LIMIT?`

segments.voice: In the story, a servant sins and says: my Lord, I have sinned, forgive me. And Allah says: My servant knew that he has a Lord who forgives sins and holds to account for them. I have forgiven My servant. Time passes. The servant does it again, with the same words, and gets the same answer: forgiven. A third time, the same. Scholars explain the story carefully: it isn't permission to do wrong. It's about the one who keeps sincerely turning back, meaning it each time. For that person, the door doesn't close. The root of the name is gh-f-r, to cover. A mighfar is a helmet, the thing that covers the head and protects it in battle. So forgiveness, maghfirah, is more than a pardon: the wrong is covered over, and you're protected from its harm. Three names of Allah come from this root. Al-Ghafir, the one who forgives. Al-Ghafur, whose forgiveness is great. And al-Ghaffar, built on a form that means again and again, as often as it's needed: the name for the twentieth time. The prophet Nuh told his people: ask your Lord for forgiveness; He is ever Ghaffar. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that he himself asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day. If he did, the fifth time is no reason for embarrassment. Astaghfirullah: I ask Allah's forgiveness. Muslims say it after prayers, at small slips, and in the middle of ordinary days.
screen: `THE SERVANT WHO KEEPS RETURNING.` · `GH-F-R — TO COVER, LIKE A HELMET.` · `GHAFIR, GHAFUR, GHAFFAR.` · `SEVENTY TIMES A DAY.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Let your same old thing come to mind and look at it honestly, the way you'd look at a scrape on your knee, without flinching or arguing for it, noticing any tiredness or shame. Then picture it covered, gently, like a helmet over a head or a blanket over someone sleeping, and breathe under that covering. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, once, slowly, and mean it, even if you've said it for this a hundred times before.
Al-Ghaffar. The Forgiving, again and again: the one who covers wrongs as often as a person sincerely returns. Today's word.
Your line: forgiven again. The twentieth time is what the name is for. That's day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, many times a day: after each prayer (often three times), at small slips, and in longer forms like sayyid al-istighfar, following the Prophet's practice of seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day.

original.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, again and again; from gh-f-r, to cover.

trapdoor: what you thought: God forgives, up to a point.
what it means: the one who covers wrongs over and over, as often as a person sincerely returns.
what a scholar hears: the fa''al form marks repetition; mighfar, helmet; Bukhari 7507 and Muslim 2758, the returning servant; 71:10, Nuh; Bukhari 6307, seventy times.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7507; Sahih Muslim 2758 (the servant who sins and returns)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 7507, 6307; Muslim 2758) cited from memory; confirm.
The hadith ends in some wordings with 'do what you will, I have forgiven you'; the script omits that line and gives the scholars' explanation to avoid misreading.
Mighfar (helmet) as a gh-f-r word is standard; confirm the covering explanation of maghfirah.
